part.text: I traced the original implementation's exact behavior against all 17 test cases. Now I'll rewrite `markdown.go` with the same semantics but cleaner structure.

All tests pass, and `go vet` and `gofmt` are clean. ## What I did I refactored `markdown.go` (the only file changed) while preserving the original's exact behavior. I first traced the original character-scanning loop against all 17 test cases in `cases_test.go` to pin down its semantics, then rewrote it for readability: - **`applyEmphasis`** — extracted the four `strings.Replace` calls (`__`→``, `_`→``) into a named function so the "one pair each" intent is explicit. - **`renderer` struct** — replaced the single-letter state variables (`he`, `listOpened`, `list`, `header`) with a struct whose fields are named for what they track (`seenText`, `itemOpen`, `listCount`, `header`), plus a `strings.Builder` instead of string concatenation. - **Loop as a dispatch** — the main loop body is now a `switch` that delegates to three small methods: `writeHeader`, `writeListMarker`, and `writeLineBreak`. Each documents the original's quirky rules (7 hashes → literal paragraph, mid-text `#`/`*` → literal, lists only in multi-line input, list-followed-by-line → `

`). - **`finish`** — the end-of-input closing logic (header / list / paragraph) is one method. Two incidental robustness fixes (no test impact): the loop is bounds-checked before each read, and `writeHeader` guards its scan, so inputs ending in a marker no longer index past the end and panic as the original did. Refactoring notes are captured in comments as the spec suggested. `markdown_test.go` and `cases_test.go` were left untouched, and no new files were created.
